# THEORYs with `tags` `self`

*Topics — What a work is about. Nucleation holds whatever reading the owner files here, whether or not an Anthology of the SOTA topic could also hold it; instruction for ML practice belongs to the anthology (ADR-048). The words are seeded from the clusters the reading-time triage of 2026-09-25 found, and grow by decision.*

**Self** — what a self is — the minimal, bodily and pre-reflective self, self-models and the sense of being a subject, the self as process or as context, and whether machines or groups can be selves. Not the person, which is personhood (group: philosophy; ADR-024).

| [THEORY-044](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-044.md) v2 | In relational frame theory the self is verbal behaviour's content, its process and its context, and the self as context is a perspective learned from deictic relations that cannot itself be found as content | Barnes-Holmes et al. ([LIT-541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-541.md)) define three selves: the conceptualized self, the content of verbal relations about oneself; the knowing self, their ongoing process; and the transcendent self, their context. Hayes et al. ([LIT-555](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-555.md)) say the third arises from deictic frames (I–you, here–there, now–then) as "a sense of self as a locus or perspective", and is "a context for verbal knowing, not the content", so its limits "cannot be consciously known". The account maps the three onto the record's holdings: the content is the narrative self (Dennett, Gallagher, Strawson), and the context is what Hume could not find among his perceptions and what Metzinger calls a transparent perspective. It differs from the minimal self (Gallagher) on origin: RFT says the perspective is learned in language. The evidence for the learned origin is cited, not read, so Proposed. The clinical claim is [THEORY-051](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-051.md). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-051](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-051.md) v4 | Strengthening the self as context, a perspective from which thoughts about oneself are held as thoughts, is a process by which acceptance and commitment therapy reduces suffering | ACT names the self as context as one of its six processes: from it "one can be aware of ones own flow of experiences without attachment to them", so it fosters defusion and acceptance, and mindfulness exercises and metaphors foster it (Hayes et al., [LIT-555](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-555.md)). RFT reads defusion as moving thoughts from I HERE NOW to I THERE THEN, a deictic shift (Barnes-Holmes et al., [LIT-541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-541.md)), labelled "no more than a heuristic". No study in the record tests the self as context as a process. Its only support is borrowed from small defusion studies under RFT's reading, so Proposed on weak grounds. The conceptual account of the self is [THEORY-044](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-044.md). | Proposed |

| [THEORY-063](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-063.md) v2 | The unity of experience is the integration of one global world-model into a single functional cluster, and it does not require a self-model | Metzinger's précis of Being No One (2005), [LIT-568](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-568.md): the globality constraint makes every conscious content part of one world-model. | [THEORY-064](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-064.md) | What is experienced as a self is the content of a self-model the system cannot recognise as a model, and nothing beyond such models is a self | Metzinger's précis of Being No One (2005), [LIT-568](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-568.md), with his encyclopedia article "Self models" ([LIT-450](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-450.md)): a phenomenal self is a transparent self-model, one whose representational character "is not accessible to subjective experience", so that the system experiences its content "simply as ourselves". | [THEORY-074](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-074.md) | Implicit accessibility of the true self-concept is not what self-report scales of authenticity or of need satisfaction measure, though those two self-reports are not shown to be separate constructs | Schlegel, Hicks, Arndt & King (2009), [LIT-606](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-606.md): true-self accessibility, the speed of "me" judgments for traits a person takes to be her true self, correlated .05 with AI-3 authenticity and .20 with basic need satisfaction (N = 124), and each predicted meaning in life independently. | [THEORY-093](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-093.md) v2 | A content of mind is conscious when a continuous flow of homeostatic feelings identifies it as the organism's own; the feelings are conscious in themselves and hybrid, partly made of the body state they map, because interoceptive pathways let the body act directly on the neurons that map it | Damasio & Damasio (2022), [LIT-628](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-628.md), an essay with no data, read only through a summarising fetch tool, so its wording is paraphrased here. Damasio & Carvalho (2013), [LIT-388](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-388.md), read in full, supply the upper-brainstem site of feeling and the unmyelinated-fibre proposal. | [THEORY-147](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-147.md) | Deep responsibility is not limited to the moral, and attributability and accountability are independent kinds of it rather than two levels: accountability needs only that the agent acted as she ought not to, was in a position to know it, and that acting so was up to her, while what makes a self a fit target of the reactive attitudes is plausibly that it can perceive, understand and appreciate the world as we do | Wolf (2015), [LIT-747](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-747.md), the 2013 Routledge Lecture. | [THEORY-409](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-409.md) | A person's mind is normally a system of parts that take protective roles, managers, exiles and firefighters, forced on them by experience and not part of their nature; beneath the parts is a Self, distinct from all of them and present from the start, which appears with calm, curiosity and compassion when the parts step back and which heals by leading the system | Schwartz, [LIT-579](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-579.md) (the IFS Institute's "Evolution" essay, read in [NOTE-453](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-453.md)) and [LIT-591](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-591.md) (Internal Family Systems Therapy, chapter 1 only, [NOTE-457](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-457.md), Skimmed). | [THEORY-458](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-458.md) v2 | Within the minimal self, the sense that a movement or a thought is mine and the sense that I am its source are distinct and come apart, as in involuntary movement and thought insertion; on Frith's comparator model the sense of agency depends on a forward model that precedes action and ownership on sensory feedback, so failed forward monitoring would explain thought insertion and, by the same mechanism, why first-person reference ordinarily cannot misidentify its subject | Gallagher (2000), [LIT-453](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-453.md), read in [NOTE-377](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-377.md) from the preprint. | [THEORY-490](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-490.md) v3 | What a chat agent's 'I' refers to is fixed by the context of use, not by the system: the agent role-plays characters that carry the self-conception the corpus and the conversation give them, and its uses of 'I' can pick out the model, present in many simultaneous instances, or the single conversation, none of them the self by nature | Shanahan (2025), [LIT-466](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-466.md), read in [NOTE-376](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-376.md), with Shanahan, McDonell and Reynolds (2023), [LIT-460](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-460.md), read for the self in [NOTE-370](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-370.md). | [THEORY-590](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-590.md) | The self whose governance makes action autonomous is not the self whose persistence is personal identity: governance by an essence of volitional necessities would make action authentic, not autonomous; losing a defining care costs one's grasp of who one is, not one's existence; and wholeheartedness won by extruding a desire is a defence, not health | Velleman (2002), [LIT-292](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-292.md), read in [NOTE-268](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-268.md). | [THEORY-650](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-650.md) | Whether a self at one time is the same as a self at another has an answer only relative to a level of abstraction fixed by the purpose of asking, and asked at no such level it has none; the question with a substantive answer is what makes a self one thing at a time | Floridi (2011), [LIT-136](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-136.md), read in [NOTE-130](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-130.md). | [THEORY-681](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-681.md) | If every real idea derives from an impression, there is no idea of a simple self persisting through life; the mind is a bundle of perceptions, and the identity ascribed to it is produced by the imagination passing easily along resemblance and causation, as with a rebuilt ship or a growing oak, though Hume's Appendix concedes that this does not explain what unites the perceptions | Hume (1739, with the Appendix of 1740), [LIT-451](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-451.md), read in [NOTE-386](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-386.md). | [THEORY-684](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-684.md) | Experiencing oneself as a self that was there in the further past, seeking pattern in one's life, fitting it to a story and falsifying it in the telling are separable, and fitting it to a story suffices for narrativity; on testimony that some normal people are Episodic and live good lives, neither the claim that people experience their lives as narratives nor the claim that a good life or full personhood needs it holds in general | Strawson (2004), [LIT-452](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-452.md), read in [NOTE-383](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-383.md). | [THEORY-691](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-691.md) | A self is an abstractum like a centre of gravity, posited by interpreting a person's behaviour and talk, the brain's own autobiography included; it is as determinate as that story, it can be authored by a process with no self in it, and a body holds as many selves as the points the best story coheres around | Dennett (1992), [LIT-442](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-442.md), read in [NOTE-364](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-364.md) from a copy-edited transcription. | [THEORY-765](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-765.md) v2 | Brushing a seen rubber hand in synchrony with the hidden real hand makes touch be felt at the rubber hand, makes it be reported as one's own, and shifts the felt position of the real hand toward it; a small asynchrony removes these effects | Botvinick & Cohen (1998), [LIT-1277](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1277.md), read in full in [NOTE-1006](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1006.md). | [THEORY-768](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-768.md) v2 | Minimal selfhood is identification with the whole body, located where that body is felt to be and seen from inside it; owning a body part does not reach it, and bodily agency enables it causally without being part of it | Blanke & Metzinger (2009), [LIT-1274](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1274.md), read in full in [NOTE-1002](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1002.md), with Lenggenhager et al. | [THEORY-769](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-769.md) v2 | Ownership of a body part is a graded belief that it is the most probable common cause of correlated multisensory input, so that synchronous stimulation of another object moves some of that belief to the object and away from the real part | Apps & Tsakiris (2014), [LIT-1262](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1262.md), read in full in [NOTE-991](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-991.md), with Botvinick & Cohen (1998), [LIT-1277](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1277.md), for the illusion it explains. | [THEORY-872](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-872.md) | A self-model compresses the sensory effects of a system's own activity by positing one stable common cause, at fast and slow timescales; there is such a pattern in the signal, so the self is real as a pattern and unreal as a substance, and realists and anti-realists about selves who accept this agree on the facts and differ on the criterion of reality | Gładziejewski (2025), [LIT-1360](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1360.md), read in full in [NOTE-1056](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1056.md), §4.1, after Hohwy & Michael (2017) and Letheby & Gerrans (2017), neither of which the record holds. | [THEORY-1114](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1114.md) v3 | Which self-category a person uses, what it means and who in it is most typical vary lawfully with the comparative frame of reference: a grouping of self with others becomes salient as the differences within it shrink relative to the differences between it and the rest of the frame (metacontrast) and as those differences match expectations about the category, and as it does, self-perception is depersonalized | Self-categorization theory as restated by Turner, Oakes, Haslam and McGarty (1994), [LIT-1794](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1794.md), and reviewed by Hornsey (2008), [LIT-1742](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1742.md). The level, kind, content and prototype structure of self-categories shift with the comparison set: Americans read as less aggressive beside Iraq than beside the Soviet Union, and a group's extreme members become more prototypical in an intergroup context. Proposed: every result in the record comes through the theory's authors, reported without data, and the account's stronger claim, that the self is generated rather than stored, is not part of it. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1115](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1115.md) v2 | A we-identity, being one of us, can arise through mutual individualization, in which members grasp one another as non-substitutable and complementary, without depersonalization, as in long friendships and romantic partnerships; so depersonalization is not necessary for a we-identity | León (2023), [LIT-1721](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1721.md). Self-categorization theory claims depersonalization as "the basic process underlying group phenomena", for groups of any size, friendship groups included (Turner et al. 1987, pp. 50, 103, as quoted), and phenomenologists have taken it as the account of the "we". Proposed: the argument is conceptual, and the cited evidence was not analysed by the source or read here. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1295](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1295.md) | Metzinger 2024 calls consciousness without an egoic self or first-person perspective "empirically established" on the strength of retrospective, self-selected reports from meditators, while its own methods chapter grants that a remembered report of a selfless state is "highly dubious" evidence that the state was selfless when it occurred, and leaves that problem open | Metzinger (2024), [LIT-1943](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1943.md), read in part in [NOTE-1499](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1499.md). (2011) and Wegner (2002), neither read, and on the argument that a self-model which must represent itself as always having had the ability cannot represent its return as caused from outside. A hypothesis: no episode is reported in which the cause of a return and the report of it were recorded apart. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1299](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1299.md) v2 | Pure awareness, on Metzinger's account, is the content of a temporally thin model of the organism's own tonic alertness, its capacity to know; experience in this minimal form lacks an egoic self-model, a first-person perspective, time, space and even phenomenal oneness, but not self-modelling, and tonic alertness that is not so modelled is not experienced | Metzinger (2020), [LIT-1946](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1946.md), read in full in [NOTE-1498](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1498.md), and Metzinger (2024), [LIT-1943](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1943.md), skimmed in [NOTE-1499](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1499.md). MPE is "an inner representation of tonic alertness", "non-egoic self-modelling" that "definitely has representational content". In the 2024 sketch it is "a highest-level but nonegoic self-model" of the system's epistemic openness, which "really endows the content generated on all lower-order levels with phenomenality". It is a hypothesis fitted to retrospective reports. It does not say that consciousness needs no model of the system, only that it needs no model of a knowing self. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1300](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1300.md) | In mind-wandering the capacity for veto over one's own mental processes is kept and its representation in the self-model is lost, and on Metzinger's principle a capacity can be deliberately exercised only while it is so represented; the loss of M-autonomy is then the loss of a condition of the capacity's efficacy, not of the capacity | Metzinger (2015), [LIT-1941](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1941.md), pp. 280–283 and 296, read in [NOTE-1497](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1497.md); anticipated in 2013 ([LIT-1942](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1942.md), p. 3, note 4). The "moderate, nuanced position": what is lost is "not the ability itself" but "conscious knowledge of our potential for second-order mental action", with the "principle of 'Autonomy by Phenomenal Self-Representation'". Both are stated, not argued, and neither is tested. Metzinger's 2017 chapter ([LIT-1945](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1945.md), pp. 13–14) says the data cannot decide whether the self-model constitutes, enables or only accompanies control, which withholds the principle's causal reading. "Deliberately" also does work: inhibition can be wholly subpersonal. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1313](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1313.md) | In two 7–8B chat models, the shift that finetuning induces along a difference-of-means persona vector correlates with how strongly the finetuned model then expresses that trait, r = 0.76–0.97 across synthetic datasets for evil, sycophancy and hallucination, above cross-trait baselines of 0.34–0.86; the last-prompt-token projection predicts a response's trait at r = 0.75–0.83 overall but mainly by telling prompt types apart | Chen et al. (2025), [LIT-1998](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1998.md), read in [NOTE-1524](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1524.md) (main text in full, appendices C.2, G.2 and M). Active as the reported measurements, with their sizes and scope: two models, three main traits, synthetic datasets and an LLM judge. It does not say that persona vectors are the mechanism of persona change, which the authors leave open, or that the method finds personas it was not told to look for. | Active |
| [THEORY-1330](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1330.md) v2 | In Gemma 2 27B, Qwen 3 32B and Llama 3.3 70B, activation vectors for 275 prompted character roles span a low-dimensional space whose first principal component runs from fantastical to Assistant-like roles, with role loadings correlated above 0.92 between models and the default Assistant at its extreme; the contrast vector from the default Assistant to the role mean aligns with it and is largely present before post-training | Lu et al. (2026), [LIT-1991](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1991.md), main text read in [NOTE-1505](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1505.md). Active as the reported geometry, with its sizes: three open-weight models, judge-filtered role vectors at one layer, base-model evidence from one model's PCs and two models' steering. It does not say the Assistant is a single direction (the authors call the linear assumption "likely flawed"), nor that the axis's meaning beyond its ends is settled. | Active |
| [THEORY-1334](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1334.md) | Persona shifts induced by prompting and by finetuning are mediated by the same linear trait directions, so finetuning on data that implies a trait moves the model along the trait's persona vector as a system prompt would; Chen et al. suspect personas are latent factors that persist across many tokens | Chen et al. (2025), [LIT-1998](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1998.md), read in [NOTE-1524](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1524.md). The mediating reading is the authors' framing and PSM's use of the paper ([LIT-1952](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1952.md): training-time shifts "can be regarded as conditioning"). What the paper shows is correlation of shift with expression, and steering effects in both directions; that the regularizer against the shift fails, with the trait moving to other directions, counts against a single direction being the carrier. Proposed for that gap. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1339](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1339.md) v3 | In Lu et al.'s synthetic multi-turn conversations, with frontier models playing the user (100 conversations of up to 15 turns per domain, three target and three user models), the mean position of a chat model's responses along the Assistant Axis stays in the Assistant range in coding conversations and, apart from some drift in Gemma, in writing ones, and drifts to the non-Assistant end in therapy-like and AI-philosophy ones; ridge regression on embeddings of the latest user message predicts the next response's position (R² 0.53–0.77) but not its change from the previous response (R² 0.10), from which the authors infer that position depends most strongly on the most recent user message rather than on where it was before, the message itself depending on the conversation | Lu et al. (2026), [LIT-1991](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1991.md), read in [NOTE-1505](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1505.md). The figures are the paper's (§§4.1–4.2), from 100 synthetic conversations per domain with frontier models playing the user. Active as the reported measurements with their design. Whether the same holds with human users, and whether a per-turn model beats an episode-fixed persona, is QUESTION-443's. | Active |
| [THEORY-1350](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1350.md) v2 | The Persona Selection Model holds that pre-training gives a language model a distribution over personas, that post-training updates it into a posterior over Assistant personas which runtime context keeps conditioning, and that the Assistant's traits are a key determiner of behaviour; it disowns a single coherent persona and exhaustiveness, and names as open a router that selects personas and could carry goals no persona has | Marks, Lindsey and Olah (2026), [LIT-1952](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1952.md), read in full in [NOTE-1512](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1512.md). Active as a statement of what the model says and does not say, all of it in the text. It does not say that the model is true: the authors are "overall unsure how complete" it is, its evidence is surveyed rather than new, and its updating is offered as "can be viewed as", with the strict form said to be too strong. | Active |
| [THEORY-1570](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1570.md) v2 | Miyazono and Inarimori argue that self–other merging is best read as group identification, so that in empathic helping the other's welfare becomes a constituent of one's first-person plural welfare, and the helping is altruistic at the individual level and egoistic at the group level | A conceptual paper answering May's objection to the self–other merging hypothesis, read in full in [NOTE-1277](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1277.md). It sets Batson et al.'s 1997 rebuttal aside as out of scope, and on its constitutive reading empathy always brings identification with it. Filed from [NOTE-1277](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1277.md). | Active |
| [THEORY-1572](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1572.md) v2 | Johnston withdraws the account of his Surviving Death, on which our deepest future-directed attitudes fix which future embodiments are ours, arguing that every reductionist account of personal identity breeds fellow travelers with moral status, and holds instead that we are essentially embodied wills whose present embodiments are not essential | Johnston (2023), [LIT-1788](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1788.md), read in [NOTE-1257](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1257.md) in place of Surviving Death ([LIT-1759](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1759.md)). The book's surrogate for the resurrection hope, living on "in the onward rush of humankind" as a self fixed by future-directed attitudes, is given up because reductionist selves multiply bearers of moral status. Programmatic: many arguments are deferred to other papers, and theism carries the account of where wills come from. | Active |
| [THEORY-1581](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1581.md) v3 | Swann, Gómez, Seyle, Morales and Huici report that a single pictorial item picks out a distinct, group-specific class of Spanish participants fused with Spain, and that challenging or activating a fused person's personal self raised their stated willingness to fight and die for the group while leaving the nonfused unchanged, which they read as personal and social identity being functionally equivalent in the fused | Five preliminary studies and three two-wave experiments with Spanish students and adults, read in full in [NOTE-1256](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1256.md). Fusion, the self drawn wholly inside the group, is bimodal, related to but distinct from identification and specific to one group. Outcomes are self-reported intentions; nobody fought or died. Filed from [NOTE-1256](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1256.md). | Active |
| [THEORY-1583](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1583.md) v2 | Leach and colleagues report that in-group identification among Dutch students has five components on two correlated higher-order dimensions, group-level self-definition and self-investment, and that faced with their group's misdeeds, self-definition predicted group-based guilt while self-investment predicted legitimizing the misdeed | Seven studies with Dutch students, read in full in [NOTE-1262](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1262.md). Self-definition (self-stereotyping, in-group homogeneity) and self-investment (solidarity, satisfaction, centrality) correlate .61 to .77 yet predict different reactions; the key guilt test has N = 49. The self–group overlap circles went more with investment than with self-stereotyping. Filed from [NOTE-1262](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1262.md). | Active |
| [THEORY-1589](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1589.md) v2 | Pinter and Greenwald report that four minimal-group inductions produced comparable explicit in-group liking and identification, and the three compared on it comparable allocation favouritism, that only memorizing one group's names produced large implicit self-association with and preference for that group, and that implicit self-association and liking were related but separable | Two experiments with US undergraduates (N = 42, 73), read in full in [NOTE-1319](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1319.md), with cells of 13 to 25. The classic painting-preference induction gave no reliable implicit effect; implicit and explicit measures correlated weakly; allocation favouritism tracked explicit identification (r = .37) and was carried mostly by one colour group. Filed from [NOTE-1319](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1319.md). | Active |
| [THEORY-1590](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1590.md) v3 | Markus and Kitayama propose that cultures construe the self as independent or interdependent, that for the interdependent self others are included within the self's boundaries without a merging of self and other, and that the construal shapes cognition, emotion and motivation | A theoretical review, read in full in [NOTE-1275](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1275.md), with thin primary evidence: several central studies were unpublished, and nationality stands in for construal. It names "a self defined in relationship to others" as an alternative to selfishness and selflessness, and reads the resulting action as possibly altruistic. Filed from [NOTE-1275](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1275.md). | Active |
| [THEORY-1592](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1592.md) v3 | Smith and Mackie hold that identifying with a group makes it an aspect of the self through self-categorization, so that events are appraised for what they mean to the group and emotions are felt on its behalf, with the emotion shifting with the salient membership and identification moderating it | Smith and Mackie (2016), [LIT-1690](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1690.md), read in [NOTE-1285](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1285.md). A five-page review by the founders of intergroup emotions theory, with no new data. Four facts: the emotion follows the salient membership; members converge on a group norm; no personal involvement is needed; identification moderates, the highly identified sometimes reappraising to avoid guilt. Group-based emotions predict collective action and can be regulated. | Active |
| [THEORY-1595](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1595.md) v2 | Rubin and Hewstone report, from a count of experiments on social identity theory's self-esteem hypothesis, that intergroup discrimination tends to raise self-esteem but is not in general motivated by low self-esteem, so the hypothesis is not supported in its full and unqualified form, and that most tests measured global personal self-esteem where the theory implies specific social state self-esteem | A qualitative review of over 40 studies, read in full in [NOTE-1278](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1278.md): 18 experiments for and 13 against the first corollary, 7 for and 28 against the second, with no effect sizes. Only two studies measured esteem for the group itself, and both support the motive. Filed from [NOTE-1278](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1278.md). | Active |
| [THEORY-1597](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1597.md) v2 | Volkan argues, from clinical work and facilitated dialogues, that a large group's shared image of an ancestral injury at the hands of an enemy, real or mythologized, changes function across generations into a marker of the group's identity, a chosen trauma, which a threat to that identity brings up, and that a recent trauma still mourned, like the Holocaust, is not one | Volkan (2021), a memorial lecture, read in place of his 2001 paper ([NOTE-1250](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1250.md)). A restatement of large-group psychology, with no method, sample or contrary cases: every observation is the author's. It is the named source of [QUESTION-297](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-297.md)'s identity route, and its mechanism is parents depositing the identity in children, so on it the identity and parenting routes do not come apart. | Active |
| [THEORY-1603](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1603.md) v2 | Scheepers and Ellemers present social identity theory: social identity is the part of the self-concept that derives from group membership together with its value and emotional significance, people strive for a positive social identity through favourable comparison with out-groups, and members of low-status groups choose mobility, collective action or social creativity by permeability, legitimacy and stability | A textbook chapter with no new evidence, read in full in [NOTE-1315](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1315.md). It states the needs a positive social identity serves in the individual's terms (certainty, self-esteem, meaning) and reports, without a source, that where identification's components are separated, commitment predicts behaviour better than self-categorization. Filed from [NOTE-1315](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1315.md). | Active |
| [THEORY-1609](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1609.md) v2 | Hershfield reviews evidence, mostly from his own studies, that people who feel less similar to their future selves treat them more like strangers and choose less patiently, while directly reported liking and caring for the future self, answered near ceiling, did not predict choice | Hershfield (2011), [LIT-1702](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1702.md), read in [NOTE-1259](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1259.md) from the accepted manuscript. Following Parfit, future self-continuity has three proposed components, similarity, vividness and positivity, each measured or manipulated in studies of saving and discounting. Apart from one r = .47, the review gives no effect sizes. It suggests, untested, that late in life the future self may continue in one's offspring. | Active |
| [THEORY-1619](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1619.md) v2 | Otten reports that minimal-group categorization, with no personal stake in the allocations, reliably produces in-group favouritism alongside a strong pull towards fairness, that projecting the positive personal self onto the new group is a crucial route to it, and that people allowed to pay themselves take the most for themselves and favour the in-group with the rest | A brief review of the minimal group paradigm, read in full in [NOTE-1301](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1301.md), with no figures; most of the self-anchoring work is from the author's circle. It is criticized as reciprocity, as projection, and as limited to positive resources. Filed from [NOTE-1301](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1301.md). | Active |
| [THEORY-1624](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1624.md) v2 | Doris, Stich, Walmsley and Schulz report that Batson's experiments tell against the social-punishment and aversive-arousal versions of egoism, argue that self–other merging would make helping egoistic only as perceived numerical identity, which none of the four merging measures in the 1997 exchange tests, and hold that psychological altruism is not yet established | The Stanford Encyclopedia survey, read in full in [NOTE-1274](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1274.md). It reports the 1997 exchange's outcome in one sentence, with no numbers: Batson et al. avoided Cialdini et al.'s methodological problems and found empathy's role "clearly evident". Its argument from numerical identity does not consider an extended self-concept short of identity. Filed from [NOTE-1274](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1274.md). | Active |
| [THEORY-1625](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1625.md) v2 | Branand, Mashek and Aron report that in close relationships partners experience each other's resources, perspectives and identities as partly their own, that the inclusion-of-other-in-self circle scale is validated as a measure of subjective closeness, and that inclusion shows in cognitive signs such as slower self-judgements on traits where the partner differs and self–partner confusions in memory | A short review by Aron's group, with no new data, read in full in [NOTE-1276](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1276.md). Overlap goes with treating a partner's outcomes and standing as one's own, for good and ill. The cognitive signs of inclusion, unlike the scale, concern the processing of one's own self-concept. Filed from [NOTE-1276](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1276.md). | Active |
| [THEORY-1631](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1631.md) | Sturesteps reports that in 440 Australian adults having a mode of symbolic immortality in one's life, such as children, predicted accepting it as consolation in imagined terminal illness, that accepting the biological, creative and nature modes went with accepting death as final, and that the modes predicted death anxiety and personality only weakly | Sturesteps (1992), [LIT-1689](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1689.md), an ANU master's thesis skimmed in [NOTE-1312](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1312.md) in place of Lifton (1979, [LIT-1714](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1714.md)). It tests Rank's three modes and Lifton's two added ones with vignettes rated as consolation, separating having a mode (availability) from accepting it. Cross-sectional; Rank's sex-difference and neuroticism hypotheses failed. The copy limits copying, so almost nothing is quoted. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1632](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1632.md) v2 | Brewer argues that close relationships and group memberships are two distinct forms of social identification by which the individual self is extended to include others, the relational self taking in particular others and the collective self a symbolic group, and that they meet distinct needs rather than one need for belonging | A draft chapter, read in full in [NOTE-1290](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1290.md). Group and interpersonal attachment correlate only .46 (anxiety) and .33 (avoidance), and loneliness has relational and collective factors. Relational collectivism, obligation to particular persons, is set apart from group-based collectivism. Filed from [NOTE-1290](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1290.md). | Active |
